changes.details: A small cove below the wooded Rumassala headland, between Galle harbour and Unawatuna, reached by a short path through the trees. newExperiences.name: Stilt fishermen at Koggala and Ahangama
newExperiences.shortDescription: See the stilt fishermen on their poles in the shallows east of Galle. Many now pose for paid photos, so agree on any payment first.
newExperiences.details: Fishermen sit on a crossbar tied to a single pole in the shallows and cast for small fish, a method dating from about the Second World War. Some still fish, mainly in the south-west monsoon months, but in the tourist season many by the road pose for photographs and ask for payment, and some are not fishermen. Agree on any payment first and don't climb a pole uninvited. Usually a short roadside stop.
newExperiences.where: Koggala and Ahangama, about 25–40 minutes east of Galle Fort on the coast road
newExperiences.season: Posing for photos most days in the tourist season; real fishing mainly about May to October
newExperiences.notes: Requested by you (villa site: stilt fishing 'on availability' on the Whale Watching Mirissa & Galle tour; guide places them 'around Koggala and Ahangama'). Destination: Galle rather than Mirissa because Koggala (about 14 km) and Ahangama (about 18 km) are in Galle District, closer to Galle Fort than to Mirissa for Koggala (Mirissa–Koggala is about 20 km), and they cluster with Koggala Lake, the Martin Wickramasinghe museum and Handunugoda as one 'east of Galle' half-day; the Galle guide already covered them. From Mirissa it is about 25–40 minutes the other way, so the Mirissa guide now points to the Galle page. No official/government source on stilt fishing found; facts rest on The National (2024), ICSF (pandemic-era report from Koggala) and The Diplomat (2018). Payment amounts deliberately omitted. Don't present it as a working-fishery 'authentic' experience, and don't imply the tour includes it.

newExperiences.name: Koggala Lake boat trip
newExperiences.shortDescription: A boat trip on Koggala Lake, a mangrove-fringed lagoon dotted with islands, with stops at a cinnamon island and a temple island.
newExperiences.details: A broad lagoon behind the coast at Koggala, scattered with small islands and fringed with mangroves. Trips of about 1.5–2 hours usually stop at an island where cinnamon is peeled (with a shop) and a temple island with old murals, and pass Madol Doova, the island behind Martin Wickramasinghe's novel. Cormorants and herons are common. Ask for life jackets; mornings and late afternoons are cooler.
newExperiences.where: Koggala, about 14 km (usually 25–35 minutes) east of Galle Fort
newExperiences.notes: Not an official source; Life.lk (2020s feature) and Lonely Planet agree on islands, cinnamon island, temple island and trip length (LP 90 min; Life.lk about 2 h). Island count varies (8 or 10). Boats are run by local operators and hotels; safety standards unknown. Pairs naturally with galle-martin-wickramasinghe-museum and galle-stilt-fishing.

newExperiences.name: Martin Wickramasinghe Folk Museum, Koggala
newExperiences.shortDescription: The birthplace of the Sinhala novelist Martin Wickramasinghe and a large museum of village life, crafts and ceremonies at Koggala.
newExperiences.details: Run by the trust set up after Martin Wickramasinghe died in 1976, the complex at Koggala includes the house where he was born, furnished with his belongings, and pavilions of folk crafts, rural tools, fishing and farming gear and ceremonial objects. Most visitors spend about an hour. Opening hours are on the trust's website.
newExperiences.where: Koggala, about 14 km (usually 25–35 minutes) east of Galle Fort
newExperiences.notes: Trust website (checked Nov 2026) says open daily 9 am–5 pm except the two-day Sinhala and Tamil New Year holiday; not quoted on the card. 'About an hour' is a typical-visit estimate from travel listings, not an official figure — remove if you prefer.

newExperiences.name: Handunugoda tea estate (white tea)
newExperiences.shortDescription: Visit a low-country tea estate inland from Ahangama, known for its white tea, to see the processing and taste the teas.
newExperiences.details: A family-owned estate in the low hills inland from Ahangama, known for its white tea. Visits usually include a walk in the plantation, a look at the small factory and a tasting of several teas, ending at the shop. Unlike the hill-country estates, it grows tea close to sea level, so it is an easy add-on to a coast day. Check the visiting arrangements before you go; allow about 1–2 hours.
newExperiences.where: Inland from Ahangama, about 40 minutes east of Galle Fort
newExperiences.notes: No official estate website found (web-search budget ran out mid-audit). Lonely Planet and several blogs describe free tours with tasting; 'free' not stated on the card. Stories that the white tea is 'untouched by human hands' are marketing — not used. Verify current visiting arrangements before publishing.

newExperiences.name: Unawatuna beach
newExperiences.shortDescription: Swim at Unawatuna, a crescent bay sheltered by headlands and a reef, a short drive from Galle Fort. Calmest from about November to April.
newExperiences.details: A curved bay between two headlands, sheltered by a reef and usually calm enough for swimming from about November to April. It is lined with cafés and guesthouses and gets busy in season; Jungle Beach and the peace pagoda are on the headland to the west. From about May to September the sea is often rough, so follow the flags and any lifeguards.
newExperiences.where: Unawatuna, about 6 km (usually 15–20 minutes) east of Galle Fort
newExperiences.notes: Sri Lanka Tourism names Unawatuna among the best southern beaches. Beach width has varied with erosion since 2004; avoid promising 'wide sand'.

newExperiences.name: Handloom weaving and natural dyeing workshop
newExperiences.shortDescription: Watch cotton being dyed and woven on wooden handlooms at a small workshop near Hikkaduwa, with a shop selling the finished cloth.
newExperiences.details: Small family workshops in the Hikkaduwa and Galle area weave cotton on foot-treadle handlooms, and some colour the yarn with plant dyes such as turmeric or tree bark. A visit shows the dyeing and the looms at work and usually ends in a shop, with no obligation to buy. Most visits take under an hour. How 'herbal' the dyes are varies from workshop to workshop.
newExperiences.notes: Requested by you. No workshop called a 'herbal cloth weaving & colour factory' could be identified near Hikkaduwa. What exists: (1) family handloom workshops near Galle with natural-dyed cotton, e.g. Sooriya Weaving at Wanchawela, about 7 km from Galle (Tripadvisor/ExcursionMania: women weavers, natural dyes, short visits, shop; no formal tours), and a 'family-run studio on the outskirts of Galle' sold through Teardrop hotels; (2) batik workshops, which Time Out says Hikkaduwa and Galle are known for; (3) a 'natural silk factory' with showroom at Gintota, a standard free stop on Hikkaduwa tuk-tuk excursions. The villa text (spinning, dyeing, looms, sold on the spot, free entry) fits (1) or a hybrid; 'factory'/'free entry' with a shop is typical of commission-based stops. Keep the card generic, without 'where', until the owner names it. Category local-life (crafts); 'culture' would also work. Do not imply the tour includes it.

newExperiences.name: Snorkelling on the Hikkaduwa reef
newExperiences.shortDescription: Snorkel from the beach over the shallow reef of Hikkaduwa National Park, with reef fish and often turtles. Calmest from about November to April.
newExperiences.details: The reef at the north end of the beach is a marine national park, on average only about 5 m deep. Much of the coral has been damaged by bleaching and heavy use and is being restored, but reef fish are plentiful and green turtles are often seen. Snorkel on calm days in the marked areas, keep your fins off the reef and never touch coral, which is prohibited. Turtle sightings are never guaranteed.
newExperiences.season: About November to April, on calm days
newExperiences.notes: DWC lists Hikkaduwa for snorkelling and boat safari. Any park entry charge for snorkellers not confirmed — not mentioned. Glass-bottom boats deliberately not proposed as a card (reported reef-top damage); they stay in the guide, described neutrally.

newExperiences.name: Surfing and surf lessons
newExperiences.shortDescription: Surf Hikkaduwa's reef breaks, or learn on the gentler waves further south around Narigama. The season runs from about November to April.
newExperiences.details: Hikkaduwa's surf season follows the north-east monsoon, roughly November to April. The reef breaks off the main beach suit experienced surfers, while the softer waves around Narigama are where most schools give lessons and rent boards. Reef and rock lie close to the surface at some breaks, so ask locally about the day's conditions and stay within your ability.
newExperiences.notes: Sri Lanka Tourism gives November–March; Wikipedia October/November–March/April. 'About November to April' matches the guide.

newExperiences.name: Scuba diving: reefs and wrecks
newExperiences.shortDescription: Dive the reefs and wrecks off Hikkaduwa, including the Conch, an oil tanker lost in 1903. Best in the calmer months, about November to April.
newExperiences.details: Dive centres in Hikkaduwa run boat dives to deeper reefs and several wrecks in the calmer months, roughly November to April, including the Conch, an oil tanker wrecked in 1903. Beginners can take introductory dives and courses. Choose a centre registered with Sri Lanka Tourism and affiliated with an international training agency, and check its equipment and boat safety gear.
newExperiences.notes: Sri Lanka Tourism mentions 'several wrecks' off Hikkaduwa. Conch date from a dive-operator blog only (one source) — re-check or drop the year. SLTDA treats diving as a water-based adventure activity for registration; could not confirm a specific dive-centre licensing rule (web-search budget exhausted), so the text gives it as advice, not as a legal requirement.

changes.name: River safari and Ambalangoda masks
changes.shortDescription: A mangrove boat trip on the Bentota River, or on the Madu River at Balapitiya further south, which pairs well with the mask museums of Ambalangoda.
changes.where: Bentota River at Bentota; Madu Ganga at Balapitiya, about 20 km south; masks at Ambalangoda, about 25 km south
changes.details: Two different rivers. Bentota River boats wind upstream from the river mouth between mangroves and islets for one to three hours. The Madu Ganga at Balapitiya, about 20 km south, is a Ramsar-listed estuary with an island temple, and Ambalangoda's mask museums are a short drive beyond. Birds and water monitors are common, crocodiles occasional. Some boats offer photos holding a captive young crocodile; decline.

changes.shortDescription: Jet skis, water-skiing, banana boats and windsurfing on the sheltered Bentota River near the mouth. Ask for a briefing and wear a life jacket.

Operators vary: ask for a safety briefing, wear a life jacket that fits, keep jet skis well clear of swimmers and fishing boats, and don't go out after drinking. The sea itself is calmer from about November to April.

newExperiences.name: Lunuganga, Geoffrey Bawa's garden
newExperiences.shortDescription: Tour the country garden of the architect Geoffrey Bawa, shaped over decades on a former plantation inland from Bentota.
newExperiences.details: Bawa bought the former rubber and cinnamon estate in 1948 and spent decades shaping it into terraces, lake views and pavilions. The Geoffrey Bawa Trust shows it only on its own guided tours at set times each day; outside guides are not allowed. Expect steps, steep slopes and uneven paths. Times, booking options and photography rules are on the Trust's website.
newExperiences.where: A short drive inland from Bentota
newExperiences.notes: Trust page (Nov 2026): garden tours daily at 11:00, 14:00 and 15:00, no reservation needed; private and curatorial tours booked ahead; third-party tours not permitted; publishing photos needs written approval. Not quoted on the card. Exact distance from Bentota not confirmed — 'short drive'. Kind 'attraction' with where; change to 'excursion' if the drive is more than about 20 minutes.

newExperiences.name: Brief Garden (Bevis Bawa's garden)

newExperiences.details: Bevis Bawa began the garden on a former rubber estate near Kalawila and developed it until his death in 1992. It is looser and more personal than Lunuganga, with sculpture, terraces and shady paths, and has long been open to visitors. Check that it is open before going; most people spend about an hour.

newExperiences.name: Surf lesson at Weligama

newExperiences.details: Weligama's long, sandy bay has soft, forgiving waves and many surf schools, which makes it one of Sri Lanka's most popular places to learn. newExperiences.name: Matara forts and Dondra Head lighthouse
newExperiences.shortDescription: See Matara's Dutch forts and the 49 m lighthouse at Dondra Head, the southernmost point of Sri Lanka, a short drive east of Mirissa.
newExperiences.details: Matara keeps a Dutch rampart fort by the sea and the small Star Fort of the 1760s, built to guard the river crossing and restored by the Department of Archaeology. Dondra Head, about 6 km beyond, is the island's southernmost point; its 49 m white lighthouse was completed in 1890. Most people take two to three hours for both, including the drive.
newExperiences.where: Matara, about 20 minutes east of Mirissa, and Dondra Head, about 6 km further
newExperiences.notes: Wikipedia only (two articles); no official tourism page checked. Whether visitors can climb the Dondra lighthouse is not confirmed — not claimed. The Paravi Duwa island temple in Matara could be added if verified. 'Two to three hours' is an estimate.

candidates.recommendation: Not a separate destination page. Cover it from Mirissa: the surf-lesson card (mirissa-weligama-surf-lesson) and the 'Along the coast' bullet.
candidates.summary: A town on a long, sandy bay about 5 km west of Mirissa (Matara District, about 144 km from Colombo), with a large fishing fleet and one of Sri Lanka's best-known beginner surf beaches. Many travellers stay there instead of Mirissa, but what it offers beyond surfing is covered by the Mirissa page, and it is 10–15 minutes away.
attractions: Weligama Bay beginner surf and surf schools
Taprobane, a tiny island with a private villa built by Count de Mauny
Kushtarajagala (Kusta Raja Gala), a 3 m rock-cut bodhisattva relief of about the 6th–9th century (single source)
Beeralu lace-making (Portuguese-introduced household craft)
Stilt fishing on the nearby coast
candidates.routes: On the A2 and the Colombo–Matara coastal railway (Weligama station). About 5 km/10–15 minutes from Mirissa, about 30 km/45 minutes–1 hour from Galle. Same route position as Mirissa (Galle → Mirissa → Yala/Udawalawe).
candidates.season: About November to April for calm seas and surf lessons; rough in the south-west monsoon.

candidates.recommendation: Not needed as a destination. Its sights are already proposed as Galle excursions (stilt fishing, Handunugoda tea estate, Koggala Lake, Martin Wickramasinghe museum).
candidates.summary: A small coastal town about 18 km east of Galle in Galle District, with surf breaks, villas and surf-camp accommodation strung along the A2. Its interest for a private-tour visitor is the stretch it shares with Koggala, which fits a half-day from Galle or a stop between Galle and Mirissa.
attractions: Stilt fishermen (Koggala–Ahangama stretch)
Handunugoda tea estate (white tea)
Martin Wickramasinghe museum, about 4 km west at Koggala
Koggala Lake
Kataluwa Purvarama temple with 19th-century murals (single source)
Surf breaks (Ahangama, Midigama)
candidates.routes: On the A2 and the coastal railway, about 18 km/30–40 minutes from Galle and about 15 km/25–30 minutes from Mirissa.
candidates.season: About November to April for the sea; the stilt fishermen fish mainly in the south-west monsoon months.

candidates.recommendation: Not a separate page now. Mentioned in the Mirissa guide; reconsider only if the owner serves surf travellers there.
candidates.summary: A small horseshoe bay just outside Dikwella (Matara District, about 22 km east of Matara), known among surfers and younger travellers. No coverage on Sri Lanka Tourism's beach page; mainly blog and operator coverage. Nearby are the Hummanaya blowhole and the Wewurukannala temple's giant seated Buddha.
attractions: Hiriketiya bay surf break
Dikwella beach, sheltered by headlands and reef
Hummanaya blowhole at Kudawella (spray up to about 25–30 m in big swell)
Wewurukannala Vihara, Dikwella, with a 50 m seated Buddha (temple name not confirmed in the source read)
candidates.routes: About 32–35 km/45 minutes–1 hour east of Mirissa via Matara; about 15–20 km west of Tangalle. Lies on the coast road towards Yala.
candidates.season: About November to April for calmer seas; check locally for surf conditions.

proposedExperiences.name: Hummanaya blowhole
proposedExperiences.shortDescription: Watch the sea burst through a rock blowhole at Kudawella, east of Mirissa, best when the swell is big. A short walk from the road.
proposedExperiences.details: At Kudawella, near Dikwella, waves force water up through a crack in the rocks, throwing spray as high as 25–30 m when the swell is big and much less on calm days. There is a viewing platform and a small visitor centre. Keep behind the barriers and away from wet rock edges. Often combined with Hiriketiya or the Wewurukannala temple.
proposedExperiences.where: Kudawella, near Dikwella, about 45 minutes to an hour east of Mirissa
proposedExperiences.season: Most active when the swell is big; ask locally
proposedExperiences.notes: Single source (Wikipedia). Which months are best could not be confirmed (often said to be the south-west monsoon). 'Keep behind the barriers' assumes barriers exist — verify. Move to a Tangalle page if one is created (it is 12 km from Tangalle).

candidates.recommendation: Own destination page, medium priority — but only if the owner routes guests along the coast to Yala. Otherwise mention it from Mirissa.
candidates.summary: A town on one of the island's largest bays (Hambantota District, about 195 km from Colombo and 35 km east of Matara), with quieter beaches than the south-west coast and a different set of sights: Rekawa, which the Department of Wildlife Conservation lists as a turtle-watching site where wild turtles nest at night; the Mulkirigala rock temple; the Hummanaya blowhole; and Kalametiya's lagoons. Sri Lanka Tourism names 'Tangalla' among the best southern beaches. It sits on the coast route from Mirissa to Yala, so it works as a one- or two-night stop.
attractions: Tangalle bay and beaches; Parewella natural swimming area
Rekawa turtle watching (DWC-listed): five species nest on the beach at night; wild, never guaranteed
Mulkirigala Raja Maha Vihara: cave temples on a 205 m rock, Kandyan-era paintings, about 20 km north
Hummanaya blowhole, Kudawella, about 12 km
Kalametiya bird sanctuary (lagoons and mangroves), about 24 km east
Dutch fort (now a prison), rest house and court house in town
Hiriketiya and Wewurukannala (Dikwella) to the west
candidates.routes: About 45 km/1–1.25 hours east of Mirissa; about 75–80 km/1.5–2 hours to Tissamaharama for Yala (estimate); Udawalawe roughly 1.5–2 hours via Embilipitiya (estimate); airport about 3–3.5 hours via the Southern Expressway (estimate). Natural stop between Mirissa and Yala.
candidates.season: Calmest seas about November to April. Rekawa nesting occurs through much of the year; peak months not confirmed.

proposedExperiences.name: Night turtle watching at Rekawa
proposedExperiences.shortDescription: Wait on Rekawa beach at night for wild sea turtles coming ashore to nest. Watch quietly, without flash; sightings are never guaranteed.
proposedExperiences.details: Sea turtles, five species in all, come ashore on Rekawa beach east of Tangalle to nest at night, and the Department of Wildlife Conservation lists it as a turtle-watching site. You wait until a nesting turtle is found, then watch from a distance with dim red light or none, no flash and no touching. Some nights bring several turtles, others none.
proposedExperiences.where: Rekawa, about 10 km east of Tangalle
proposedExperiences.notes: Only if a Tangalle page is created (destinationId 'tangalle' does not exist yet); from Mirissa it is too far for a night visit (about 1.5 hours each way). Who runs the watch (community programme/TCP with DWC) and current visiting arrangements need confirming. This is wild nesting, unlike the Kosgoda/Hikkaduwa hatcheries.

proposedExperiences.name: Mulkirigala rock temple
proposedExperiences.shortDescription: Climb past cave shrines with Kandyan-era paintings and reclining Buddhas to the top of a 205 m rock north of Tangalle.
proposedExperiences.details: A cave-temple complex on a 205 m rock, by tradition about 2,000 years old and enlarged under the Kandyan kings in the 18th century. Steep steps lead up past several cave shrines with Kandyan-era paintings of the Buddha's life and reclining Buddha images. It is a working temple: cover shoulders and knees and remove shoes. Allow about two hours, and go early before the rock heats up.
proposedExperiences.where: Mulkirigala, about 20 km north of Tangalle
proposedExperiences.notes: Wikipedia only (two articles). The Mahavamsa attributes the founding to King Saddhatissa (Wikipedia says 'third century'; most chronologies put him in the 2nd century BC) — hence 'by tradition about 2,000 years'. Number of steps not confirmed. Only if a Tangalle page is created; otherwise it is about 1–1.25 hours from Mirissa.
